items.title: Myanmar vows to defy ‘inappropriate’ measures in Rohingya genocide ruling
items.summary: The leader of the Myanmar military-backed government said it will refuse to comply with some aspects of a landmark international court ruling that found the country responsible for genocide against the Rohingya minority. President Min Aung Hlaing told a Cabinet meeting that his government would act accordingly but would reject measures it considered “inappropriate,” the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar newspaper reported on Thursday. The president on Wednesday described the case as a “one-sided accusation” against the country, and said the use of the term “genocide” had seriously damaged Myanmar’s reputation. The International Court of Justice, the United Nations’ top court, ruled last week that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in a brutal 2017 military operation. The court found that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence and acts of extreme violence against children. The court rejected Myanmar’s defense that the campaign was a legitimate operation against insurgents. Min Aung Hlaing, the former military leader, was in charge of the operation. The report said that Min Aung Hlaing considered himself primarily responsible for all matters concerning Myanmar as the country’s leader, and would not accept actions that undermined the nation. “Myanmar would take the actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate,” he said, without elaborating. Myanmar’s government earlier described the International Court of Justice’s decision as unfair and a great disappointment , pointing out that six of the 15 judges had dissented. The ruling was the first time the international court has ruled that a state committed genocide. It ordered Myanmar’s government to allow the Rohingya to return home safely, pay reparations and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide. The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council. Myanmar is considered unlikely to fulfill any of the court’s demands. The separate International Criminal Court, or ICC, also based in The Hague and considering legal action concerning Myanmar and the Rohingya, is under U.S. sanctions along with many of its judges and staff, so any action by the Security Council could face a U.S. veto. items.title: Why the Siang dam protests matter beyond Arunachal
items.summary: Inevitably, when one story dominates the news cycle, many other developing stories get buried or even forgotten. This column is to remind you of one such story, a story that began in 1982 in Arunachal Pradesh, a state about which we know precious little, barring the fact that it borders China. Those of us who live in the ‘mainland’ became aware of unrest in this border state recently when locals came out in numbers to protest a large dam project on the Siang river. In one instance, in the town of Pasighat , on the banks of the Siang, the protest turned violent; arrests were made, and people supporting the protests were intimidated. Why should protests against a dam in Arunachal Pradesh interest people in the rest of the country? Because these protests are not just about one dam. They remind us, yet again, that successive governments continue to push policies where people, mostly from indigenous communities, and the environment are considered the necessary “collateral damage” in the larger national interest. In the case of Arunachal Pradesh, an additional wrinkle is “strategic interests”, as stated by Home Minister Amit Shah during his recent visit to the state. As a result, when villagers ask questions, they have been intimidated, arrested, and their villages have been turned into “military zones”, as described in this story in Scroll . The 1,200-MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP), the government argues, is essential because China is building an even bigger dam further upstream. This, it claims, will help India ensure that the release of water from the upstream dam can be regulated and not flood downstream areas located in Arunachal Pradesh. All this sounds reasonable if you do not know the record of large dams in highly seismic areas such as the Upper Siang region, or the poor implementation of resettlement and rehabilitation for affected communities in many similar projects in India. In this case, the dam will submerge 27 villages, displace an estimated 1.5 lakh people who belong to the Adi tribe, the second largest in Arunachal Pradesh, and erase what they consider to be their ancestral lands. The Indian Express has published a comprehensive report with videos that highlights the social costs of this project. A familiar struggle Anyone who has followed the trajectory of large dams in India would be familiar with the struggle against the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada River in Gujarat, which began in the 1980s. items.summary: Months after releasing the latest National Family Health Survey (NFHS) factsheet without crucial data on anaemia, the Union government has finally published the figures under a separate study. They were released on Tuesday, November 24, in a study titled the Survey for Assessment of Markers of Population Health, Activity, Diet and Anthropometry (SAMPADA) 2023–2025. The data show that nearly 56% of women of reproductive age (15-49 years) are anaemic, despite a systematic intervention through Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB), a strategy launched in 2018. The Union Ministry, however, said that severe anaemia was observed only in less than 2% of people in the majority of the age groups. The report was prepared by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) under the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. While the government claimed that the prevalence of anaemia came down, experts point out that results of SAMPADA are not comparable with previous national surveys. An analysis of the Union Government’s scheme Anaemia Mukt Bharat, against the backdrop of survey results, shows nearly half of the funds remain unutilised. The Anaemia Mukt Bharat strategy, launched in 2018, aimed to reduce anaemia among children, adolescents, pregnant and lactating women and women of reproductive age through various interventions, including the distribution of iron folic acid supplements. According to the WHO, it is diagnosed when blood haemoglobin levels fall below specific thresholds set by age, sex, and physiological status. Anaemia is a serious global public health problem that particularly affects young children, menstruating adolescent girls and women, and pregnant and postpartum women. As per the new study, the prevalence of anaemia in children aged 12-59 months is 42%. items.title: EXCLUSIVE: चीनी कंपनी को ठेके, जनता को कचरे का पहाड़! गुरुग्राम के बंधवाड़ी लैंडफिल का पूरा सच
items.summary: गुरुग्राम की कचरे की समस्या का समाधान सालों पहले हो जाना चाहिए था. लेकिन ऐसा होने के बजाय यह नाकाम कॉन्ट्रैक्ट और सरकारी पैसों की बर्बादी का एक अंतहीन सिलसिला बन गया. 2017 में एक प्राइवेट कंपनी इकोग्रीन को गुरुग्राम और फरीदाबाद में कचरा इकट्ठा करने और उसे वैज्ञानिक तरीके से प्रोसेस करने का ठेका दिया गया था. इस कंपनी में एक चीनी कंपनी ने 428 करोड़ रुपये का निवेश किया. वहीं, सरकार ने इकोग्रीन को 157 करोड़ रुपये का भुगतान भी किया. लेकिन जिस वेस्ट-टू-एनर्जी प्लांट का वादा किया गया था, वह कभी बना ही नहीं. दूसरी तरफ, बंधवारी लैंडफिल पर कचरे का पहाड़ बढ़ता गया और आसपास के गांवों का भूजल प्रदूषित होता रहा. गौरतलब है कि इकोग्रीन 2017 तक गाजियाबाद के अग्रवाल परिवार की एक निष्क्रिय कंपनी थी. उसी साल एक चीनी कंपनी ने इसमें 99.98 फीसदी हिस्सेदारी खरीद ली. इसके महज छह महीनों के भीतर कंपनी को लखनऊ, ग्वालियर और गुरुग्राम-फरीदाबाद में कचरा प्रबंधन के ठेके मिल गए. कंपनी की वित्तीय फाइलिंग से पता चलता है कि गुरुग्राम प्रोजेक्ट में शुरुआती 60 करोड़ रुपये के निवेश का करीब 80 फीसदी हिस्सा संबंधित कंपनियों और पक्षों को ट्रांसफर कर दिया गया. वहीं, चीनी कंपनी के 428 करोड़ रुपये के निवेश के मुकाबले जमीन पर महज 60 करोड़ रुपये की प्लांट और मशीनरी ही मौजूद है. आखिरकार 2024 में चीनी कंपनी ने इकोग्रीन में अपनी पूरी हिस्सेदारी महज एक करोड़ रुपये में बेच दी और भारतीय बाजार से बाहर निकल गई. 2024 में इकोग्रीन का कॉन्ट्रैक्ट रद्द होने के बाद सरकार ने इस गड़बड़ी को ठीक करने के लिए नौ और कंपनियों को 532 करोड़ रुपये के ठेके दिए. इनमें से छह कंपनियां तय समयसीमा में अपना काम पूरा नहीं कर पाईं और उन पर करीब 20 करोड़ रुपये का जुर्माना लगाया गया. इसके बावजूद सरकार इन कंपनियों को 311.5 करोड़ रुपये का भुगतान कर चुकी थी. इसके बाद गुरुग्राम में कचरा प्रबंधन के लिए 600 करोड़ रुपये से ज्यादा का एक और टेंडर जारी किया गया. गुरुग्राम के बंधवाड़ी में कचरे का पहाड़ लगातार बढ़ रहा है और इसके साथ बढ़ता जा रहा है सरकारी खजाने पर बोझ. करोड़ों रुपये खर्च होने के बावजूद समस्या जस की तस है और एक बार फिर वही सिलसिला शुरू हो चुका है. आखिर इस पूरे खेल में किसे फायदा हुआ और इसकी कीमत कौन चुका रहा है? देखिए हमारी यह खास पड़ताल. भ्रामक सूचनाओं के दौर में आपको ऐसी खबरों की जरूरत है, जिन पर आप भरोसा कर सकें. न्यूज़लॉन्ड्री आपके लिए ऐसी ही खबरें लेकर आता है. हमारी पत्रकारिता को मजबूत करने के लिए सब्सक्राइब करें. गुरुग्राम: हिंसा, आगजनी और पत्थरबाजी के कारण अब तक 250 परिवारों का पलायन हरियाणा: मोनू मानेसर, अफवाह और पुलिस की लापरवाही बनी नूंह से गुरुग्राम तक सांप्रदायिक हिंसा की वजह?

items.title: What Tata Trusts’ suits in Bombay High Court say against N Chandrasekaran’s reappointment
items.summary: Trustees of the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and the Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT) have filed a suit before the Bombay High Court challenging a board resolution passed by Tata Sons Private Limited on September 17. That resolution has sought to reappoint Natarajan Chandrasekaran as the Executive Chairman of Tata Sons for another five years. The resolution was passed 4:1. Directors Venu Srinivasan, Harish Manwani, Anita M George and Saurabh Agrawal voted in favour. Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata voted against it while Chandrasekaran abstained. Tata Trusts, which controls 66% stake in Tata Sons, has argued that the reappointment resolution is void ab initio. They have sought a declaration that the resolution is ultra vires the Articles of Association and, hence, null and void. It has sought an order to restrain the company from acting on the reappointment. SDTT has also sought a bar on the board chair casting vote when 2 trust nominees disagree. Relief has been sought ahead of the November 30 board meeting. The trusts have collectively sought damages to the tune of ₹65 crore: ₹50 crore by SDTT, and ₹15 crore by RDTT. Here is a summary of the suits filed before the High Court. Named defendants The suit names the following defendants: Tata Sons; Natarajan Chandrasekaran; Saurabh Agrawal; Harish Manwani; Anita George; Venu Srinivasan; and Noel N Tata (no reliefs sought against him) Board meeting under scrutiny Chandrasekaran e-mailed the board on August 12, 2026, stating he would not seek reappointment when his term ends on February 20, 2027. SDTT and five other trusts passed resolutions on August 13 respecting that decision and asked the company to help constitute a selection committee under Article 118. At the September 17 meeting, Chandrasekaran said he had reconsidered and was willing to be appointed for another five-year term from February 21, 2027 to February 20, 2032. Two Trust directors nominated under Article 104B of the Articles of Association of Tata Sons were present: Srinivasan voted in favour, while Noel Tata objected and voted against it. Chandrasekaran recused himself as an interested director. Acting chair for the agenda, Harish Manwani, exercised a casting vote to treat the resolution as passed. Core of the dispute: Article 121 of the Articles of Association Article 121 requires “the affirmative vote of a majority of the (Trust) Directors appointed pursuant to Article 104B present at the meeting" on matters decided by a majority of directors. items.title: Delhi HC slams MHA for not disclosing "secret" inputs that led to cancellation of NGO's FCRA license
items.summary: The Delhi High Court on Thursday criticised the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) for not disclosing, even to the court, the “security inputs” which formed the basis for cancellation of the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA) registration of NGO Socio-Legal Information Centre (SLIC). SLIC is a non-governmental organisation (NGO) that describes itself as a legal aid and education organisation. In his order, Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani noted that the NGO faced drastic action because of these security inputs, adding that they cannot be kept secret to the point that no material is shown even to the Court. “While the respondent [government] contends that the violations on the appellant’s [NGO’s] part were brought to its notice through ‘security inputs’, which cannot be divulged since they are ‘secret’; this court is of the view that such inputs cannot be kept secret to the point that no material is brought even to the notice of this court, though the appellant has faced the drastic action of having its FCRA registration cancelled, arising from such inputs,” the Court said. The Court quashed the government’s order cancelling the NGO’s FCRA registration and pulled up the authorities for stating that the NGO portrayed “wrong image of public institutions of India in the eyes of international community.” Justice Bhambhani said that such an allegation strains credulity and the Court is dismayed by the government’s "attempt to baselessly portray the appellant organisation in such light” . “This court is further of the view that the impugned cancellation order is misconceived, untenable and illegal, apart from being disproportionate and excessive in its rigour and impact,” the Court concluded. It added that Section 14(2) of the FCRA requires a personal hearing before cancellation of registration, and that merely issuing a show-cause notice is insufficient given the serious consequences. items.title: Saket court acquits former My FM CEO of sexual harassment charges
items.summary: A Delhi court on Monday acquitted Harish M Bhatia, former CEO of My FM, the radio arm of the Dainik Bhaskar Group, of the charges of outraging and insulting the modesty of a woman. Judicial Magistrate First Class Shivangi Vyas of Saket courts held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court reiterated that a conviction in a sexual offence can be based solely n a complainant's testimony only if the same is of sterling quality. "The conviction in a sexual offence case can be based solely on the testimony of prosecutrix provided her testimony is of sterling quality that is wholly reliable, consistent and inspires confidence," it said. Where the case rests primarily on that testimony, the Court must scrutinize it with greater care to ensure that it is free from material contradictions, improvements, omissions or inherent improbabilities, the judge added. Since the same was not satisfied in the present case, Bhatia was acquitted of all charges. The complainant, then National Programming Head, alleged harassment between 2008 and 2010 at the workplace, office parties and tours. Her final allegation concerned May 7, 2010, when Bhatia allegedly called her to his cabin, held her hands and demanded sexual favours. He was booked for offences under Sections 354 (assault with intent to outrage modesty) and 509 (word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The Court found three conflicting versions about her resignation. In her complaint she said it was forced, in her testimony she denied sending any resignation, and in her first complaint to the National Commission for Women she said she resigned on grounds of ill health. The Court held that they were all contradictory to each other. It also noted that the allegations in her testimony were far graver than those in her complaint. items.title: Small mercies and large silences: The Supreme Court and the Constitution at 77
items.summary: Every November 26, the Supreme Court’s lawns are scrubbed, the ceremonial speeches are dusted off and the Republic congratulates itself on the durability of its founding charter. Constitution Day invites easy theatrics. Critics declare the document dead on arrival; loyalists hail the bench as an infallible shield against executive excess. The Supreme Court’s record across 2026 resists both caricatures. Over the past 11 months, the Court has displayed a striking split personality. When confronting the daily, retail indignities inflicted on ordinary citizens by municipal apathy, police high-handedness or bureaucratic drift, the Court has been remarkably imaginative. Yet, when asked to scrutinise the institutional architecture of democracy itself, the same Court has repeatedly blinked, deferred or stalled in the vestibule. The guardian of the sidewalk Take the Court’s record on individual dignity and personal liberty this year and there is genuine constitutional craftsmanship to admire. In June, while hearing a petition on road safety, a bench elevated something Indians routinely treat as an urban luxury into an enforceable right. It held that walking safely on unobstructed, demarcated footpaths flows directly from Article 19(1)(d) and Article 21, imposing binding obligations on civic authorities. For citizens forced onto speeding carriageways because municipalities surrender pavements to encroachments, reading that basic mobility into the Constitution was no trivial gesture. That instinct to police everyday abuses carried steadily through the autumn docket. Earlier this month, in Sri Sujit Das , the Court closed a favorite loophole of investigative agencies. It ruled that the constitutional 24-hour clock under Article 22(2) for producing a detainee before a magistrate begins ticking from the moment liberty is actually curtailed , not whenever an officer records a formal arrest. Days later, in Devilal Gond , it ordered compensation for a man kept languishing behind bars for over seven years after his High Court acquittal because administrative paperwork moved slower than human despair. Nor did the Court shy away from hard moral and ecological questions affecting vulnerable communities. In March, while permitting the withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment in Harish Rana , it fixed the practical bottlenecks in constituting medical boards so that the right to die with dignity would cease to be trapped in bureaucratic purgatory. items.title: Tryst with the Constitution: Parliament must debate
items.summary: In his final address to the Constituent Assembly, Dr BR Ambedkar famously remarked that the success of a Constitution depends, in large measure, on the people who are called upon to work it. If they happen to be a ‘good lot’, even a bad Constitution may turn out to be good. The functioning of the Constituent Assembly, the intellectual rigour of its deliberations and, more importantly, the attitude of its members proved that they were indeed such ‘good people’. 77 years later, as we celebrate Constitution Day, we must revisit the spirit of deliberation that characterised the making of our Constitution. Deliberation, dissent, consensus A remarkable feature of the Indian Constitution is the extent to which it was discussed and debated before it took its final shape. Prior to the appointment of the Drafting Committee, the Assembly constituted numerous committees to examine specific aspects of the Constitution and make recommendations. These recommendations, as approved by the Assembly, formed the basis of the initial draft prepared by Sir BN Rau, which was subsequently scrutinised and revised by the Drafting Committee led by Dr Ambedkar. Before being taken up for discussion by the Assembly, the Draft Constitution was published and widely circulated among members of the Assembly, provinces, the judiciary and the public, inviting their comments and suggestions. The Drafting Committee considered these submissions and revised several provisions accordingly. The Assembly itself devoted 114 of its 165 sitting days to the consideration of the Draft Constitution, during which 2,473 amendments were moved. This exercise was not a mere formality. Members often identified shortcomings in the provisions and proposed amendments, several of which were accepted by Ambedkar. For instance, the Draft Constitution empowered the State to impose restrictions on several freedoms, including the freedom to form associations, move freely, reside and settle in any part of India, acquire, hold and dispose of property, and practise any profession, without clear limits on the breadth of these restrictions. Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava proposed the insertion of the word ‘reasonable’ , arguing that the restrictions imposed by the legislature must be amenable to judicial review. A Bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi made the observation while issuing notice to the State of Uttar Pradesh on a an appeal challenging the High Court verdict. The Court tagged the matter with the pending batch of appeals arising out of the Karnataka hijab ban case . "Permission to file the petition is granted. Issue notice. Rejecting her plea, the High Court held that no authoritative religious text or material had been placed on record to establish that wearing a headscarf inside a classroom is an essential religious practice under Article 25 of the Constitution. It also noted that the Karnataka High Court's Full Bench verdict upholding restrictions on hijabs in educational institutions continued to hold persuasive value in the absence of a final authoritative pronouncement by the Supreme Court following its 2022 split verdict. The High Court further ruled that the school's past inaction or tolerance in lower classes did not create an estoppel against enforcing a uniform dress code in higher classes. items.title: Self-proclaimed journalists covering protests may not have same protection as accredited journalists: Supreme Court
items.summary: "Self-proclaimed journalists" might not get the same protection of law available to journalists affiliated to any news organisation or body, the Supreme Court remarked on Thursday [Kerala Union of Working Journalists v. Union of India]. A bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana made the observation while agreeing to examine questions surrounding protection afforded to journalists covering protests. More specifically, the Bench said it will examine whether accredited journalists enjoy greater protection than self-proclaimed journalists while covering protests. “Self-proclaimed journalists may not have the same protection as accredited journalists," Justice Bagchi observed. CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, Justice V Mohana The Court was hearing petitions filed by Kerala Union of Working Journalists (KUWJ) argued by Senior Advocate PV Dinesh and others over the alleged detention and forcible removal of journalists covering protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. Today, it disposed of a plea by the KUWJ concerning the alleged detention and manhandling of seven journalists and relegating them to the court-appointed inquiry committee without expressing any opinion on merits. The Bench also posed a number of questions on the issue, including: Who qualifies as a journalist? Should professional accreditation or institutional affiliation determine the protection available to journalists? Do journalists enjoy any special privilege vis-à-vis law enforcement agencies while covering protests? Does forcible removal of a journalist from a protest site amount to custody? What are its constitutional consequences? The Court observed that journalistic freedom must be balanced with the maintenance of public order. It indicated that it could address gaps in the existing framework governing police interaction with journalists. Further, it said that individual allegations of police excesses are to be examined by the court-appointed inquiry committee, while the Court can examine the larger constitutional questions. items.title: Supreme Court asks Centre to consider setting up multiple Adjudicating Authorities under PMLA
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday urged the Central government to consider setting up multiple adjudicating authorities to decide whether provisional property attachments by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) should be confirmed. A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana took note of the rising number of complaints and applications filed before the adjudicating authority. It added that the increasing caseload, coupled with the time-bound nature of adjudication, puts enormous pressure on the members of the adjudicating authority. items.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled that the adjudicating authority confirming the provisional attachment of properties by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) must include a judicial member. A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana also ruled that the attachment cannot be confirmed by a single-member adjudicating authority unless that member is a judicial member. The Bench observed that the adjudication carries substantial consequences for the civil and consequential constitutional rights of the person whose property has been attached by the ED. "If the Adjudicating Authority finds that the property is involved in money laundering, the provisions of Sections 8(3) and 8(4) are attracted and possession of the property is taken over by the Government of India. Such dispossession may well endure until the conclusion of the trial for the offence of money laundering, depriving the person of the use of the property for a considerable period before the offence is proved," the Court said. Thus, the Court said that the presence of a judicial member on the bench would ensure legal objectivity in the determination recorded by the Adjudicating Authority. It added that though the rich experience of the administrative or financial members of the Adjudicating Authority would undoubtedly render them exceptional experts in their fields, impartial and legally sound adjudication necessitates judicial temperament and training. items.title: TVS family dispute: Lakshmi Venu moves Madras High Court seeking partition of father Venu Srinivasan's family assets
items.summary: Lakshmi Venu, daughter of TVS Motor Company Chairman Emeritus Venu Srinivasan, has moved the Madras High Court seeking partition of the joint family assets of the Venu Srinivasan branch of the TVS family [Lakshmi Venu Vs Venu Srinivasan]. She has also sought access to documents and information concerning the family assets that were allegedly withheld from her despite repeated requests. The suit marks an escalation in the dispute between Venu Srinivasan and his daughter over the division of family wealth. The dispute centres on an arrangement reached between Venu Srinivasan, his wife Mallika Srinivasan and their children Lakshmi Venu and Sudarshan Venu in 2024. While Venu Srinivasan has maintained that a fair division was effected between his children, Lakshmi and Mallika Srinivasan have contested this position. On November 16, Lakshmi issued a partition notice to her father, calling upon him to discharge his fiduciary duties as the head of the family and effect a lawful partition. items.title: Supreme Court likely to pronounce verdict in Sabarimala reference case by December this year
items.summary: A nine-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court is likely to deliver its verdict in the Sabarimala reference case by December 18 this year. The case concerns seven larger legal questions on the scope of religious freedom in India. Justice BV Nagarathna, one of the judges on the bench, hinted that the verdict may be delivered before the Court closes for Christmas vacation on December 18. The indication came during the hearing of petitions challenging a High Court ruling on the Knanaya Catholic community’s alleged practice of expelling members who do not follow endogamous marriage customs. Since the Sabarimala verdict is likely to have a bearing on the Knanaya case, the Court proceeded to adjourn the matter and posted it for consideration in January next year. The Sabarimala reference was heard by a Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant along with Justices BV Nagarathna , MM Sundresh , Ahsanuddin Amanullah , Aravind Kumar , Augustine George Masih , Prasanna B Varale , R Mahadevan and Joymalya Bagchi. The matter is connected to the Supreme Court's 2018 verdict allowing women of all ages to enter the Sabarimala Temple in Kerala. The 2018 judgment overturned a custom restricting the entry of women of menstruating age to the hilltop shrine. In November 2019, the Supreme Court pronounced its judgment on the review petitions against the 2018 verdict, but did not decide the matter one way or the other. Instead, it framed seven larger questions touching upon religious freedoms in India for consideration by a larger bench of the Court. These included deciding on the interplay between Articles 25 (freedom of conscience and religion) and 26 (freedom to manage religious affairs) on the one hand and the right to equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. The nine-judge bench then heard the case for 16 days before reserving its judgment on May 14 this year . items.title: Tamil Nadu introduces 15-day paternity leave for government employees
items.summary: Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay on Thursday, November 26 announced 15 days of paternity leave for married male government employees, marking the first time that the state has introduced such a provision. The leave can be availed either 15 days before the birth of a child or within six months from the date of birth. An official government release said the decision was taken following requests from government employees. The new provision is intended to enable fathers to support their wives during childbirth and participate in the care and upbringing of their newborn children. The government highlighted the importance of a father’s involvement during the period surrounding childbirth, noting that both the mother and the newborn require support and care. The official release stated, “The period surrounding childbirth is crucial for both the mother and the child, and the father’s involvement in providing physical and emotional support to the mother and caring for the newborn is essential.” The announcement comes against the backdrop of the existing maternity leave provision for women government employees in Tamil Nadu, who are entitled to 365 days of maternity leave. The government said that the provision of extended maternity leave reflects the importance attached to motherhood and child welfare. Similarly, paternity leave for male employees is expected to help fathers share family responsibilities and ensure their involvement in raising children. Tamil Nadu is not the first state in India to introduce paternity leave for government employees. Odisha introduced a 15-day paternity leave provision in 2011, while West Bengal provides 30 days of paternity-cum-childcare leave to eligible male employees. Kerala provides up to 10 days of paternity leave, while Madhya Pradesh provides 15 days under its revised civil service leave rules, effective from January 2026. Assam also introduced 14 days of paternity leave for eligible male government employees in September 2026. The duration, eligibility criteria and period within which the paternity leave can be availed varies across states.

items.title: Inside Hyderabad’s oocyte harvesting network and the role of fertility clinics
items.summary: Maryam* and her husband were struggling to pay off an emergency loan of Rs 1 lakh when a friend suggested selling her oocytes – the reproductive cells or ‘eggs’ extracted from the ovaries and used in the in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) process. The friend assured that she had done this herself and gave the number of the egg donation ‘agent’, Nikhat Parvin. Nikhat was from West Bengal, like Maryam, but worked out of Hyderabad. Maryam was told that she would have to travel from Kolkata to Hyderabad at her own expense and undergo the oocyte retrieval process. If the eggs were successfully extracted, she would be paid Rs 50,000 to 70,000. Maryam discussed the offer with her husband, a teacher at a madrasa, and they decided to take it. Leaving her six-year-old child at home, Maryam took a train to Hyderabad, arriving on October 10. Once her period began, she was given hormone injections which help multiple eggs mature in a single cycle rather than just one or two. But before the oocytes were retrieved, the hostel where she was staying in Begumpet was raided by the police. Nikhat was arrested on charges of running a racket to sell human gametes, prohibited under the Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act. Nikhat and Amit Sharma, who was managing the hostel along with her, were also charged with human trafficking, cheating, criminal conspiracy, and organised crime. They were accused of acting as agents bringing egg donors to fertility clinics for money. Maryam spent nearly two weeks at shelter homes in Hyderabad before her husband could send her money to return home. “I thought I was doing a nice thing by helping another couple have a baby while also earning some money from it. I didn’t know it was illegal,” Maryam said, having returned to Kolkata with no earnings, some discomfort from the injections, and distress from the police raid and having her documents and belongings seized for the investigation. items.title: Meta meets Congress leaders after protests over bias in content moderation
items.summary: Meta executives met Congress leaders in Delhi on Tuesday, November 24, amid protests by the Indian Youth Congress (IYC) over suspended Instagram accounts and alleged bias in the platform’s content moderation. The company defended its moderation policies, maintained that it was politically neutral and made no commitments on the party’s demands, according to media reports. Meta representatives Aman Jain and Natasha Jog met Supriya Shrinate, chairperson of the Congress Social Media and Digital Platforms department, along with other party functionaries. The meeting reportedly took place at Meta’s request. The discussions came after the IYC held demonstrations outside Meta-affiliated offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram from November 20. Protests were also reported in Bengaluru on Wednesday. The youth wing accused Meta of restricting political content posted by Congress leaders while allowing similar content from the BJP to remain accessible. The IYC has issued a seven-day ultimatum to Meta, demanding the restoration of suspended Instagram accounts and the removal of restrictions. The protests followed the blocking of the official Instagram accounts of IYC president Uday Bhanu Chib and All India Congress Committee in-charge for the IYC, Manish Sharma. The accounts have since been restored. During the meeting, Meta officials explained how content moderation and restrictions operate on its platforms. They said the company applies its policies equally to all political parties and that its actions are guided by Indian law and its Community Standards. According to media reports, Meta said several moderation actions involved synthetically generated content. The company explained that this includes material created or substantially altered using artificial intelligence, machine learning and other computational tools, such as deepfakes and AI-generated text, images, audio and video. Meta also outlined the measures it uses to identify and restrict content that violates its rules. These include automated detection tools, user reports, reviews against its Community Standards and applicable Indian laws, and action on valid orders issued by authorised government agencies and courts.
